The proposed U.S. High Speed Civil Transport (HSCT) will revolutionize commercial air travel by providing economical supersonic passenger service to destinations worldwide.
Unlike the high-bypass turbofan engines that propel today's subsonic airliners, HSCT engines will have much higher jet exhaust speeds.
Jet noise, caused by the turbulent mixing of high-speed exhaust with the surrounding air, poses a significant challenge for HSCT engine designers.
Advanced mixer-ejector nozzles reduce HSCT jet noise to airport noise certification levels by entraining and mixing large quantities of ambient air with the engines' jet streams.
As the HSCT gains speed and climbs, poor ejector inlet recovery and ejector ram drag contribute to poor thrust, making it advantageous to turn off the ejector.
Turning off the ejector prematurely can cause unacceptable noise levels to propagate to the ground, even when the aircraft is many miles from the airport.
The optimizer dynamically chooses the best altitude-velocity path and throttle setting history to minimize the noise propagated to the ground at any given throttle setting.

The noise metrics used in the calculations are based on the recommendations of researchers at the NASA Langley Research Center, who have correlated the flyover noise annoyance levels of actual laboratory subjects.
The HSCT's climb noise will be characterized by relatively low noise levels, long durations, and low-frequency spectra.
Analysis of data from the optimizer has shown that significant reductions in noise may be obtained with trajectory optimization.
Only small penalties in HSCT range or fuel performance occur since throttling operations are performed in the subsonic portion of the climb path (where thrust is plentiful).
